title: A History of Western Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell
target_audience: Students and academics in philosophy and the humanities
General readers interested in Western thought
Individuals seeking an accessible overview of the philosophical tradition
Anyone exploring the progression of ideas in Western civilization
core_themes: Chronological survey of Western philosophic thought
Influence of historical and societal context on philosophy
Connections between philosophy, politics, and culture
Critical analysis and personal assessments of major philosophers
Evolution of metaphysical, epistemological, and ethical ideas
primary_purpose: To provide a comprehensive, readable account of the development of Western philosophy from the pre-Socratic Greeks to the early 20th century, highlighting key philosophers, their ideas, and their historical contexts, while offering Russell’s critical commentary and perspectives.

structure_format.narrative_style: Scholarly yet accessible, often witty and opinionated
structure_format.organization: Divided into three main books—Ancient Philosophy, Catholic Philosophy, and Modern Philosophy—further subdivided into chronological and thematic chapters focusing on individual philosophers or schools

key_concepts_lessons: Western philosophy developed in dialogue with political, scientific, and cultural changes.
Major figures such as Plato, Aristotle, Aquinas, Descartes, Locke, Kant, Hegel, and Nietzsche shaped the intellectual landscape.
Philosophy evolved from metaphysics and cosmology to epistemology and ethics.
Philosophers both reflected and influenced the values and structures of their societies.
Intellectual history is characterized by both continuity and radical shifts in perspective.
Russell emphasizes reason, skepticism, and the importance of critical inquiry throughout the tradition.
notable_features: Blend of historical exposition and personal critique
Wide historical and geographic sweep—from Ancient Greece to early 20th-century Europe
Russell’s candid assessment of both ideas and personalities
Extensive influence as an introductory text for generations of students
cultural_historical_context: Written during World War II and published in 1945, the book reflects Russell’s desire to make philosophy accessible and relevant to a broad audience, while underscoring the importance of rational inquiry in a turbulent era. Russell’s work is itself a product of 20th-century analytic philosophy, offering both a genealogy of ideas and a pointed, sometimes idiosyncratic critique of their legacy.
reception_impact: Became an international bestseller and seminal introduction to Western philosophy
Praised for its clarity, wit, and ambitious scope
Criticized for occasional bias and oversimplification; some perceived Russell’s opinions as unfair to certain thinkers
Influenced the popular conception of philosophy and inspired numerous readers to study the subject further
Remains highly cited, though now supplemented by more recent scholarship
comparable_titles: The Story of Philosophy by Will Durant
Sophie's World by Jostein Gaarder (for a younger audience)
The Passion of the Western Mind by Richard Tarnas
The Oxford History of Western Philosophy edited by Anthony Kenny
